summary: Describes how to carry IPv6 over IEEE 802.16 broadband wireless networks using the IPv6 convergence sublayer. It builds on the packet convergence sublayer for IP traffic. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: 802.16 is the wireless standard used by broadband radio networks, and it leaves the job of running IP over it to other documents. This RFC fills that gap for IPv6, saying how a packet gets from a subscriber's device to the router that serves it, and how the device learns its address and the router's settings.

subtitle: How IPv6 traffic is carried over a WiMAX-style broadband wireless link.

tldr.problem: The IEEE 802.16 standard defines the air interface, its MAC layer and its physical layers, but says nothing about how IPv4 or IPv6 work over it, so every deployment had to invent its own answer.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies IPv6 over the IP-specific part of the 802.16 packet convergence sublayer: a 6-byte MAC header in front of the IPv6 packet, a point-to-point link between each host and the access router, and its own timings for router advertisements and the maximum packet size.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 hosts on 802.16 networks gained a defined link model, prefix rules and advertisement timing, and the same rules were then applied to the WiMAX network architecture in the appendices.

today: RFC 5121 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8064, a recommendation on stable IPv6 interface identifiers. The link model, prefix rules and advertisement timings it sets for IPv6 over 802.16 still describe how a host on a broadband wireless link reaches its access router.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16e is an air interface for fixed and mobile broadband wireless access systems. The IEEE 802.16 standard specifies the air interface, including the Medium Access Control layer and multiple physical layer specifications, and it can be deployed in licensed as well as unlicensed spectrum. While the physical and MAC layers are specified in IEEE 802.16, the details of IPv4 and IPv6 operation over the air interface are not included. This document specifies the operation of IPv6 over the IEEE 802.16 air interface.

IPv6 packets can be carried over the air interface in two ways: through the IP-specific part of the packet convergence sublayer, or through the 802.3-specific part of the packet convergence sublayer. The scope of this specification is limited to the operation of IPv6 over IP CS only.

The convergence sublayers are part of the MAC, and the packet convergence sublayer includes the IP-specific part used by the IPv6 layer. The mobile station, or host, is attached to an access router via a base station. The host and the base station are connected via the IEEE 802.16 air interface at the link and physical layers. The IPv6 link from the mobile station terminates at an access router that may be part of the base station or an entity beyond it. The base station is a layer 2 entity from the perspective of the IPv6 link between the mobile station and the access router, and it relays the IPv6 packets between the access router and the host over a point-to-point connection.
sections.plainLanguage: 802.16 says how the radio link works but says nothing about IP on top of it. This RFC covers one of the two ways IPv6 can travel over 802.16, the one where the IP packet sits directly in the wireless link.

sections.title: Convergence Sublayers in the 802.16 MAC
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.16 MAC specifies two main service-specific convergence sublayers, the ATM convergence sublayer and the packet convergence sublayer. The packet convergence sublayer is used for the transport of packet-based protocols, which include IEEE 802.3 Ethernet and the Internet Protocol, both IPv4 and IPv6. The service-specific convergence sublayer resides on top of the MAC Common Part Sublayer, which handles ranging and scheduling, and below it sits the MAC security sublayer, which handles authentication, encryption and key management, and then the physical layer.

The service-specific convergence sublayer is responsible for accepting packets from the upper layer, performing classification of the packet based on a set of defined service-specific classifiers, delivering the packet to the appropriate service flow and transport connection, and receiving packets from the peer entity. Payload header suppression is also a function of the convergence sublayer but is optional.

Classifiers for each specific upper-layer protocol, Ethernet and IP, are defined in the IEEE 802.16 specification and enable packets from the upper layer to be processed by the appropriate service-specific part of the packet convergence sublayer. IPv6 can be transported directly over the IP-specific part, and IPv4 packets are transported over the same part. The IP classifiers operate on the fields of the IP header and the transport protocol, and include the IP traffic class, the next header field, masked IP source and destination addresses, and protocol source and destination port ranges. The MAC uses these classifiers to map an upper-layer packet to a specific service flow and transport connection.

Support for IPv6 over the IP-specific part is negotiated. Immediately after ranging and the exchange of the basic capability messages, the mobile station and the base station exchange their capabilities via the Registration Request and Registration Response messages. By default, Packet, IPv4 and 802.3/Ethernet are supported. IPv6 over the IP CS is supported only when the IPv6 support bit in the capability negotiation messages is indicated. During the establishment of the transport connection, the Dynamic Service Addition Request and Response messages between the base station and the mobile station indicate via the CS-Specification TLV which convergence sublayer the connection uses. The mobile station and the base station must negotiate at most one convergence sublayer for IPv6 transport on a given link, and when both support IPv6 over IP CS and over Ethernet CS they must use IP CS.
sections.plainLanguage: The wireless MAC has a layer that adapts whatever the network above it sends. For IP that layer looks at the IP header to decide which radio connection to send a packet on. IPv6 support is negotiated when the device joins the network, and the two ends must pick one way of carrying IPv6, not two.

sections.title: IPv6 Encapsulation over the IP CS
sections.content:
The IPv6 payload when carried over the IP-specific part of the packet convergence sublayer is encapsulated by the 6-byte IEEE 802.16 generic MAC header. The CRC is optional, and the actual MAC address is not included in the MAC header.

For transmission of IPv6 packets via the IP CS over IEEE 802.16, the IPv6 layer interfaces with the 802.16 MAC directly. The IPv6 layer delivers the IPv6 packet to the packet convergence sublayer of the IEEE 802.16 MAC, which defines the set of classifiers used to determine how to handle the packet. The MAC encapsulates the IPv6 packet in the 6-byte MAC header and transmits it. On the downlink, from the base station to the host, the MAC selects a transport connection for the packet using the classification rules, and the host reconstructs the packet, undoing payload header suppression if it was applied.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 packet on the radio link has six bytes of wireless header in front of it. The receiver puts the packet back together, restoring any part of the header that the radio link had stripped away to save space.

sections.title: The Access Router and the Base Station
sections.content:
In a network that uses the 802.16 air interface, the host is attached to an IPv6 access router in the network. The base station is a layer 2 entity only. The access router can be an integral part of the base station, or it can be an entity beyond the base station within the access network, and one access router may be attached to multiple base stations.

IPv6 packets between the mobile station and the base station are carried over a point-to-point transport connection identified by a unique Connection Identifier. The transport connection is a MAC layer link between the mobile station and the base station. Two architectures are described. In the first, the access router is an integral part of the base station, so the base station has one connection identifier per mobile station. In the second, the access router is separate from the base station, and the packets travel over a layer 2 tunnel between the base station and the access router.

These network models are examples, shown to illustrate the point-to-point link between the mobile station and the access router. More esoteric architectures are possible but are not considered in the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Every subscriber device has its own private link to the router that serves it. The router may sit inside the base station, or in a central place reached through the base station, in which case the packets cross a tunnel on the way.

sections.title: The IPv6 Link and How It Is Set Up
sections.content:
Neighbor Discovery for IP Version 6 defines a link as a communication facility or medium over which nodes can communicate at the link layer, the layer immediately below IP. A link is bounded by routers that decrement the hop limit field in the IPv6 header. When a mobile station moves within a link it can keep using its IP addresses. This is a layer 3 definition, and it is not identical with the definition of the term L2 link in the IEEE 802 standards.

In 802.16, the transport connection between a mobile station and a base station is used to transport user data, and a transport connection is represented by a Connection Identifier, with multiple transport connections able to exist between a mobile station and a base station. When the access router and the base station are colocated, the collection of transport connections to a mobile station is defined as a single link. When they are separated, it is recommended that a tunnel be established between the access router and the base station whose granularity is no greater than per mobile station or per service flow, since a mobile station can have multiple service flows identified by a service flow identifier. The tunnels for a mobile station, in combination with its transport connections, then form a single point-to-point link. A different prefix should be assigned to each unique link, and a unique IPv6 prefix per link must be assigned.

The link is established as part of network entry. The mobile station performs initial ranging with the base station, which is the process by which it becomes time-aligned. The two exchange basic capabilities using the SBC request and reply messages. The mobile station progresses to an authentication phase, based on Privacy Key Management version 2, and on successful completion of authentication performs 802.16 registration with the network. The mobile station and the base station then perform a capability exchange in which protocol support is indicated; support for IPv6 over the IP-specific part of the packet convergence sublayer is indicated by Bit 2 of the CS capability parameter, and by default Packet, IPv4 and 802.3/Ethernet are supported. The mobile station must request the establishment of a service flow for IPv6 packets over IP CS if both ends have confirmed the capability, and the service flow may also be triggered by the network as a result of pre-provisioning. The access router and the mobile station should then send router advertisements and solicitations as specified in Neighbor Discovery.

The maximum transmission unit for IPv6 packets on an 802.16 link is configurable, and the default should be 1500 octets. The 802.16 MAC PDU is composed of a 6-byte header followed by an optional payload and an optional CRC covering the header and the payload. The length of the PDU is indicated by the Len parameter in the generic MAC header, which has a size of 11 bits, so the total MAC PDU size is 2048 bytes. In certain deployment scenarios the MTU value can be greater than the default, and Neighbor Discovery for IPv6 defines an MTU option that the access router must advertise via a router advertisement if a value different from 1500 is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining the network takes several steps: the device times itself against the radio, agrees basic capabilities, authenticates, registers, exchanges what it can support, and asks for a service flow to carry IPv6. The router then advertises itself. The default packet size for IPv6 on the radio link is 1500 bytes.

sections.title: Prefix Assignment and Host Addressing
sections.content:
The mobile station and the access router are connected by a point-to-point connection at the IPv6 layer, so each mobile station can be considered to be on a separate subnet. A customer premises equipment type of device that serves multiple IPv6 hosts may be the end point of the connection, and one or more /64 prefixes should be assigned to a link. The prefixes are advertised with the on-link flag set as specified in Neighbor Discovery. The size and number of the prefixes are a configuration issue. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol or Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting based prefix delegation may also be used to provide one or more prefixes to mobile stations for an access router connected over 802.16.

The addressing scheme for IPv6 hosts in 802.16 networks follows the IETF recommendation for hosts specified in IPv6 Node Requirements, and that document's set of applicable RFCs is equally applicable to hosts that use 802.16 as the link layer. The mobile station has a 48-bit globally unique MAC address, which must be used to generate the modified EUI-64 format-based interface identifier. As in other links that support IPv6, EUI-64-based interface identifiers are not mandatory and other mechanisms, such as random interface identifiers, may also be used.

Duplicate Address Detection should be performed as specified in Neighbor Discovery and IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration. Because the IPv6 link over 802.16 is specified as a point-to-point link, it may be redundant to perform Duplicate Address Detection on a global unicast address, as long as two conditions are met: the prefixes advertised by the access router are unique to that link, and the access router does not autoconfigure any IPv6 global unicast addresses from the prefix that it advertises. Stateless address autoconfiguration, when performed, must follow the specifications it names, and stateful address autoconfiguration, when performed, must follow the specifications it names.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device is on a link of its own, so each link gets its own prefix, usually a /64. The device forms its address from its radio hardware address, and because nobody else can be on its private link, the duplicate address check can often be skipped.

sections.title: Router Discovery and Advertisement Timing
sections.content:
On completion of the establishment of the IPv6 link, the mobile station may send a router solicitation to solicit a router advertisement from the access router. A network-attached mobile station may also send router solicitations at any time. Movement detection at the IP layer of a mobile station is in many cases based on receiving periodic router advertisements, and the station may also detect changes in its attachment via link triggers or other means. The router solicitation is sent over the IPv6 link that has been previously established, to the all-routers multicast address, and it is carried over the point-to-point link to the access router via the base station. The station does not need to know the link-local address of the access router in order to send a router solicitation. The use of router advertisements as a means for movement detection is not recommended for mobile nodes connected via 802.16 links, because the frequency of periodic router advertisements would have to be high.

The access router should send a configurable number of router advertisements to the mobile station as soon as the IPv6 link is established, and sends unsolicited router advertisements periodically. The interval between periodic router advertisements is greater than the interval in Neighbor Discovery for IPv6.

Because 802.16 hosts can go idle, in which case the radio link between the base station and the mobile station is torn down, and paging is required if the network needs to deliver packets, the interval between periodic router advertisements should be set quite high in order to avoid waking a mobile that is idle. The router lifetime should be set to a large value, preferably in hours, and the AdvDefaultLifetime in the router advertisement must be either zero or between MaxRtrAdvInterval and 43200 seconds, with a default value of twice MaxRtrAdvInterval. The MaxRtrAdvInterval must be no less than 4 seconds and no greater than 21600 seconds, and the default value is 10800 seconds.

Multicast Listener Discovery Version 2 for IPv6 should be supported as specified by the hosts and routers attached to each other via an 802.16 link. The access router that has hosts attached to it via a point-to-point link over an 802.16 should not send periodic queries if the host is in idle or dormant mode, and the access router can obtain information about the state of a host from the paging controller in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: On a wireless network the router rarely advertises itself often, because doing so would wake up radios that are sleeping. The default gap between advertisements is 10800 seconds, and the router's lifetime is set to hours rather than seconds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document introduces no new vulnerabilities to IPv6 specifications or operation. The security of the 802.16 air interface is the subject of the IEEE 802.16 standard. The RFC notes that 802.16 provides the capability to cipher the traffic carried over the transport connections, and that a traffic encryption key is generated by the mobile station and the base station on completion of successful authentication and is used to secure the traffic over the air interface. A mobile station may still use IPv6 security mechanisms even in the presence of security over the 802.16 link. The security issues of the network architecture spanning beyond the 802.16 base stations are the subject of the documents defining such architectures, such as the WiMAX Network Architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is introduced here. The radio link has its own encryption, and a device may still use IPv6 security on top of that if it wants to.

viz.caption: THE VALUES THIS RFC SETS FOR 802.16 LINKS

items.title: Default MTU
items.text: 1500 octets for IPv6 packets on an 802.16 link. A different value must be advertised in the router advertisement.

items.title: Total MAC PDU size
items.text: 2048 bytes, because the Len parameter that carries the length is 11 bits.

items.title: MaxRtrAdvInterval
items.text: Between 4 and 21600 seconds, with a default of 10800 seconds.

items.title: AdvDefaultLifetime
items.text: Either zero or between MaxRtrAdvInterval and 43200 seconds; the default is twice MaxRtrAdvInterval.

items.title: Router lifetime
items.text: Should be set to a large value, preferably in hours, because the radio link is torn down when the host is idle.

items.title: Prefix per link
items.text: One or more /64 prefixes, unique to the link.
